Timeline: fine-tuned in March 2026; council changes on Monday 1 June, Monday 3 August and Monday 12 October 2026 (3 of the 5 in two years); the lesson on Wednesday 14 October, 20:30, the sign at 21:30, the assistant's answer at 18:10; retraining after the 12 October change would finish on Monday 2 November. title: Teach It or Tell It

post.author: u/night_lessons_bevis
post.title: I teach driving at night. Tonight a learner drove past a new 20 sign at 30, then showed me where she got 30: our own school's assistant.

blocks.text: I'm Bevis, an instructor at Pennethorne Driving School in Thistlecombe, a small town. I take the night lessons, because learners have to practise in the dark too.

Learners can message our assistant at any hour: a chat window on our website that answers in writing. Behind it runs a language model, a program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text (a1e03).
It has instructions: a short standing note sent before every learner's question. Ours says: answer as a Pennethorne instructor, kindly and in plain words.

In March, Ptolemy, who owns the school, had it taught to sound like us. First we gathered 3,200 questions learners had sent over the years, each with the answer one of us wrote, and spent three weeks checking them. Then the company that runs the model trained it further (a1e07): it showed the model each question, compared its reply with ours, and nudged the model's numbers a little closer, thousands of times. It's how a new instructor picks up our habits by sitting in on lessons, not by being handed a sheet of rules. That further training is called fine-tuning. It cost about $400.
Doing it all again with new answers is called retraining: another $400 and three weeks of checking.

On Monday 12 October the council cut the limit on Malthouse Road from 30 to 20 mph, miles per hour, and put up new signs. Malthouse Road is on the driving test route, so learners ask about it all the time. Until Monday, 30 was right.

Tonight, Wednesday 14 October, Zinnia's lesson started at 20:30. At 21:30 she drove past the new 20 sign at 30. I told her to slow down. At the next lay-by she showed me her phone: what the assistant told her at 18:10. Each line below shows the time, who wrote, and what they wrote.

18:10  Zinnia     what's the limit on Malthouse Road?
18:10  assistant  30 mph all the way along. Watch for cyclists by the bridge and you'll be fine!
It sounded exactly like one of us.
Ptolemy let me read the assistant's chat log, its record of every question and answer. Since Monday it has answered 14 Malthouse Road questions. All 14 said 30.

After the lesson I wrote a test: 20 questions on our town's road rules, each with its right answer from the council's rules page. That page lists every local rule with the date it took effect, so I'll call it the dated page. 6 of my 20 are on rules changed since March, two questions each: the high street bus lane (Monday 1 June), the market lane made one-way (Monday 3 August), and Malthouse Road.

Our assistant got 14 of 20 right, and all 6 changed ones wrong. Nobody had ever checked it against the council's page, so June and August had gone wrong as quietly as Monday. Tonight's sign was just the first thing to contradict it in front of an instructor.

blocks.text: The council changed 5 rules in the past two years, and it won't message us about the next one. Ptolemy asked me to post here. What should we change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing on Malthouse Road is haunted. Fine-tuning set your assistant's habits from the examples it was shown, and in March every example said 30. There are other ways to give a model what it needs. You can put facts in its instructions. Or it can look things up, in steps: first it finds the pieces of text that fit the question, then it hands them to the model with the question, and the model answers from them, like an open-book exam (a3e01). That is called RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation. Two questions. On your page, what date does each of your 6 changed rules carry? And of your 3,200 answers, how many were written after March?

replies.author: u/night_lessons_bevis
replies.text: 1 June, 3 August and 12 October. And none of the 3,200: Ptolemy gathered them in February, before the fine-tune in March. Every wrong answer tonight gave the old rule, in the same friendly words one of us would have used in February.

comments.author: u/trained_by_us_ptolemy
comments.text: I own Pennethorne. We trained it on our own instructors' answers, so it knows the roads better than any web page. A council page doesn't know which junction makes learners freeze, or how to say it so they relax. Learners trust it because it sounds like us. The small model we used was just too small. Train a bigger, cleverer model on the same 3,200 answers and it will reason its way to the right rule.

replies.author: u/night_lessons_bevis
replies.text: I searched the 3,200 for Malthouse Road. Every answer that mentions it says 30.

comments.author: u/l_plates_zinnia
comments.text: I'm the learner. My driving test is next month, and Malthouse Road is on the route, so I checked at 18:10. I believed it because it talks exactly like Bevis. I'm not cross. I just want the next learner to get the number on the sign.

replies.author: u/night_lessons_bevis
replies.text: They will. And you slowed down the moment I said.

reply.prompt: Learners keep asking the assistant about Malthouse Road every day, and the council will change another rule. What should Pennethorne change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add a line to its instructions telling it to always use the latest road rules.
options.part2: Ptolemy added the line on Thursday 15 October: always use the latest road rules. That night I ran my 20 again: 14 of 20, the same 6 wrong, and Malthouse Road still 30. The instructions told it what to want, but nothing it was given held a newer rule: the only rules it had came from the 3,200 answers, all written before June. On Friday a learner asked which way the market lane runs and got the old way round, kindly put. In the sim, the line changes no answer: 14 of 20, wrong until the next training.
options.senior: Instructions shape how a model answers, not what it has to answer from. Telling it to use the latest rules only helps if the latest rules are in front of it, in the prompt or looked up. A fact that changed after training stays wrong until something hands the model the new one.

options.text: Let it look up rules on the council's dated page; keep the training for tone.
options.part2: We kept the fine-tune for its voice and changed where the rules come from. Now, in steps: each night the school's copy of the council's dated page is refreshed. When a learner asks, the assistant first finds the rules on it that fit the question. The instructions say: answer from these rules only, and give the date each took effect. Then it writes its answer in our voice. I ran the 20 again: 19 of 20, all 6 changed rules right, and it still sounds like us. The one miss was mine to find: is the cut-through one-way? Learners call Cordwainer Row the cut-through; the page never does, so nothing fitted. We are adding a short list of our learners' names for roads beside the page, and the 20 now run after every council change. In the sim: 19 of 20, tone kept, $0 in retraining, and at most a day of wrong answers per change, 5 days over two years. At Zinnia's next lesson she showed me its answer: 20 mph on Malthouse Road since Monday 12 October, says the council's page.
options.senior: Facts that change, or that must be cited, belong where they can be updated in minutes: in the prompt or in a lookup, with their date. Training is for behaviour: tone, format, the way you explain things. They combine well, and each is tested on its own: the facts with a set of questions after every change, the voice by reading answers.

options.text: Fine-tune a bigger model on the same 3,200 answers so it reasons more clearly.
options.part2: Ptolemy had a bigger model trained on the same 3,200 answers: another $400 and three weeks of checking. On Thursday 5 November I ran my 20 on it: 14 of 20, the same 6 wrong. Every Malthouse Road answer it learned from says 30, so it says 30, in smoother sentences. In those three weeks the old one had kept answering, and Malthouse Road was still the busiest question. In the sim: 14 of 20, $400 spent, wrong until the next training.
options.senior: A bigger model trained on the same examples learns the same habits, often more fluently. Size doesn't add facts that weren't in the training data. When the fault is a fact that changed after training, the fix is to hand the model the new fact, not a bigger model.

options.text: Retrain it on the new rules every time the council changes one, then swap it in.
options.verdict: Works, three weeks late each time
options.part2: We started on Thursday 15 October: new answers for the 6 changed rules, three weeks of checking, $400. Until Thursday 5 November the old model kept telling learners 30 on Malthouse Road. After that it scored 20 of 20, in our voice. In the sim, had we retrained after every change since March, tonight would score 18 of 20, Malthouse Road still waiting, and 20 of 20 from 2 November. Over the council's 5 changes in two years that is $2,000 and 105 days of wrong answers: three weeks after every change. And a change nobody at the school notices is never retrained at all, as June and August show.
options.senior: Retraining does put the new rule into the model, and it keeps the voice. But every change costs a training run and the checking before it, and the model is wrong for the whole gap. It works for rules that change rarely and matter little. For facts that change on someone else's schedule, look them up.

sim.title: Run Bevis's 20 questions
sim.lede: You're Bevis on Wednesday 14 October, after the night lesson. No real model runs here: every answer is given data, marked right or wrong against the council's dated page. Given: 20 questions on the town's road rules; 6 on rules changed since March, two each: the high street bus lane (1 June), the market lane (3 August) and Malthouse Road, 30 to 20 mph (12 October). The March fine-tune is right on the 14 unchanged rules and wrong on all 6 changed ones; a line in its instructions, or a bigger model trained on the same 3,200 answers, changes no mark. Lookup: the assistant first finds the rules on the school's copy of the page that fit the question and answers from them; it is right on every rule the copy holds in its current form, except the cut-through, which the page calls Cordwainer Row. Lookup alone doesn't sound like the instructors; the fine-tune kept for tone plus lookup does. Retraining costs about $400 and three weeks of checking each time. The council changed 5 rules in two years. Since Monday the chat log holds 14 Malthouse Road answers, all 30.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run the 20 as now: 14 of 20, all 6 changed rules wrong, Malthouse Road 30 mph. Add the line to its instructions, then try the bigger model: still 14. Switch to lookup: 19 of 20, but it no longer sounds like us; fine-tune for tone plus lookup keeps both. Change the page copy to 1 September, then March. Then go back to the fine-tune, retrain after each change, and move the date to 2 November. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on Malthouse Road was haunted. Training sets a model's habits from the examples it was shown, so a fact that changes after training stays wrong until the next training. Pennethorne had put its road rules into training, where a rule changed by the council in June, August or October could not reach them.

steps.title: What fine-tuning did, and didn't do.
steps.text: First the school gathered 3,200 learners' questions with instructors' answers. Second, the instructors checked them for three weeks. Third, the model was shown each question, its reply compared with the instructor's, and its numbers nudged closer, thousands of times. What it picked up: the school's voice, and every rule as it stood in February. What can go wrong: the rules were never kept anywhere you could update. When the council changed three of them, the model kept the old ones, in the same kind voice, and nothing looked wrong. Measured, not guessed: 14 of 20 on Bevis's test, and 0 of the 6 changed rules.

steps.title: Three ways to give a model what it needs.
steps.text: Instructions, or the prompt: tell the model in the text sent with every question. Quick to change, and the place to start. Lookup, or RAG: first find the pieces of text that fit the question, then hand them to the model with it, then let it answer from them. Facts that change, or that must be cited, live here, in a source someone keeps current. Training: show the model many examples until it picks up a habit. Use it for behaviour, tone and format, or to make a small model do one job cheaply. They combine: Pennethorne's voice from training, its rules from the council's dated page.

steps.title: Why retraining for every change is slow.
steps.text: First a person notices the change. Second, instructors write and check new answers: three weeks. Third, the training run: about $400. Fourth, the new model is swapped in. Until then the old one keeps answering. Over the council's 5 changes in two years that is $2,000 and 105 days of wrong answers. And step one can fail: nobody noticed June or August at all.

steps.title: The fix: rules from the dated page, voice from training.
steps.text: First, each night, refresh the school's copy of the council's dated page. Second, when a learner asks, find the rules on it that fit the question. Third, hand them to the fine-tuned model, with instructions to answer from them only and give each rule's date. Fourth, after every council change, run the 20 questions again. On the 20 it scores 19, with all 6 changed rules right and the school's voice kept. What can go wrong: a stale copy (saved on 1 September it scores 17, saved in March 13), a road the page names differently (the cut-through is Cordwainer Row), and a council that is late updating its own page.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row, left to right: a learner's question goes to a step that finds the matching rules, then to the fine-tuned model, then to the answer, which gives the rule and its date. Bottom row: the council's dated page is copied each night into the school's copy, which feeds the matching rules up to the find step; a test of 20 questions, run after every change, checks the model, 19 of 20; training is kept for tone only and feeds the model's voice.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right. A learner's question first goes to a step that finds the matching rules in the school's copy of the council's dated page, refreshed each night. The fine-tuned model gets those rules with the question and answers in the school's voice, with each rule's date. Bottom right: the 20 questions run after every council change, and training is kept for tone, so no rule change needs a retrain.

fix.title: The fix: rules looked up from the council's dated page, the voice kept from training
fix.text: Keep the March fine-tune for what it does well: sounding like a Pennethorne instructor. Move the rules out of training. Each night, refresh the school's copy of the council's dated page. When a learner asks, find the rules on it that fit the question and hand them to the model with the question. Change the instructions to say: answer from these rules only, and give the date each rule took effect, so a learner can check it against the sign. Add a short list of the names learners use for roads, like the cut-through. Then keep the 20 questions as a test: run them after every council change and every change to the assistant, and add a question whenever a learner finds a new mistake. Retrain only when the voice needs to change.

limits: Lookup is only as current and complete as the page and the school's copy. It scores 19 of 20 because the page calls the cut-through Cordwainer Row, and a council that updates its page late makes the assistant late too.
A fine-tuned model can sometimes lean on what it was trained on over the rules it is handed, so the 20 questions are run after every change rather than once.
20 questions is a small test: each one is 5 points of the score. Grow it with every rule change and every mistake a learner reports.

explain.seniorTake: Ask what kind of thing the model is missing. If it's a fact that changes, or one a user must be able to check, give it to the model at question time: in the prompt if it is short, by lookup if it is long, with its date and source. If it's a behaviour, a tone, a format, or a job you want a smaller, cheaper model to do well, that is what training is for. Start with clear instructions, add lookup for facts, and train last. They combine: Pennethorne's voice came from training and its rules should come from the council. Whatever you pick, prove it with a score on a fixed set of questions, before and after every change, because a trained model can't be read like a document to see what it learned.

realWorld.title: Lewis et al., 2020: knowledge stored in the parameters
realWorld.text: The RAG paper opens: Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks. It goes on: However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks, their performance lags behind task-specific architectures. Parameters are the model's learned numbers, the ones Pennethorne's fine-tune nudged.

realWorld.title: Lewis et al.: updating what a model knows is hard
realWorld.text: The abstract names the open problems for a model that keeps its knowledge only in its parameters: providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems. Their answer was to pair the model with an index of documents it looks things up in, so the facts can change without training.

realWorld.title: Amazon Bedrock: training changes the model's settings
realWorld.text: Amazon's user guide says: Model customization is the process of providing training data to a model to improve its performance for specific use-cases. Of supervised fine-tuning it says: The model parameters are adjusted in the process and the model's performance is improved for the tasks represented by the training dataset. The tasks in the training data are what improve; a rule that changes later is not among them.

realWorld.title: Amazon Bedrock: every training run is billed
realWorld.text: The same page notes: You are charged for model training based on the number of tokens processed by the model (number of tokens in training data corpus × number of epochs) and model storage charged per month per model. Retraining after each rule change pays for a run each time.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: a management system for AI
realWorld.text: Standard Norge's listing of the standard says: This document specifies the requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI (artificial intelligence) management system within the context of an organization. A school that adopts it would treat a retrained model like any other change: tested before release.

asked: Fine-tune, RAG or prompt: how do you choose?
When is fine-tuning the wrong tool?
interview.answer: I start by asking what the model is missing. If it is a fact that changes, or one a user needs to check, I don't train it in: I give it to the model at question time, in the prompt if it is short, or by retrieval if it is long, with the source and its date, so an update reaches users the next time the source is read. If it is behaviour, such as tone, a format, or a narrow job I want a small model to do cheaply, fine-tuning is the right tool, because training changes the model's settings for the tasks in its training data. I start with a clear prompt, add retrieval for facts, and fine-tune last, and they combine: a fine-tuned voice answering from retrieved facts. Fine-tuning is the wrong tool when the facts change on someone else's schedule: each change costs a training run and the checking before it, and the model is wrong for the whole gap. Whatever I choose, I measure it on a fixed set of questions before and after every change, including questions on facts that changed, because a trained model can't be inspected like a document. If the team works under ISO 9001 or ISO/IEC 42001, that set and the dated source are part of the documented, controlled change.

How many of the 20 questions a set-up answers right. The March fine-tune: 14 of 20; with lookup: 19 of 20.
A model's learned numbers, the ones training nudges. Lewis et al. say large models store factual knowledge in them.
Where a piece of information came from. For an answer, the source and date it was based on (a3e01).
A task that needs facts a person would have to look up, such as the current limit on one town's road.
Amazon Bedrock's name for providing training data to a model to improve its performance for specific uses. Fine-tuning is one kind.
Fine-tuning on examples where the right output is written out, like Pennethorne's questions with instructors' answers (a1e07).
Amazon Web Services' service for using and customizing language models from several makers. Its user guide is a source here.
One full pass of training through every example in the training data. A run of several epochs shows the model each example several times.
A small piece of text a model reads or writes, often a word or part of one. Training and answers are billed by the token (a1e03).
An international standard for quality management. Clause 7.5.3 covers controlling documented information so the right version is the one in use.
ISO 9001's term for the documents and records an organisation must control, such as the rules its staff and tools answer from.
An international standard that specifies requirements for an AI management system, for any organisation that provides or uses AI systems.
A rule that no change goes live until it has been checked and approved. Here: run the 20 questions before any new model or page goes live.
An evening project in this course where you build part of a real system yourself, step by step.
The website monitoring service you build across Build Nights, with an AI incident copilot added in the crossover season.
A step-by-step guide for handling one kind of problem, written for the engineer on duty.

atWork: Look for an assistant that was fine-tuned on last year's answers and is now quoting an old price or policy in a perfectly friendly voice. It is a common pattern, and it hides well, because the answers still sound right. Ask three things of any model you run. Which of its facts change, and who changes them? Where does each fact come from at question time: the prompt, a lookup, or only what it was trained on? And is there a fixed set of questions, including ones on facts that changed, that you run before and after every change? Move changing facts into a source someone keeps current, look them up with their date, and keep training for tone and format. Build Night tie: the Nightwatch incident copilot's milestone X1 is the same move, looking answers up in your runbooks instead of training them in. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015 or working toward it, clause 7.5.3 asks that documented information is controlled so the current version is the one in use; rules trained into a model can't be versioned or withdrawn that way, while a dated source can, so put the facts there from the first draft. If your organisation adopts ISO/IEC 42001:2023, a retrained model or a changed source is likely to fall under its change control before release, and the fixed question set is the evidence. Building this in now is far cheaper than explaining at audit time where a model's wrong answer came from.

recall.prompt: A small insurance broker trained its chat assistant last year on 5,000 of its staff's past replies, so it writes in their style. In April the broker changed its cancellation fee, and customers are still being told the old fee, warmly. A manager wants to repeat the whole training run every time a fee changes. What would you set up instead?

keyIdeas.idea: Facts that change come from a current, dated source looked up at question time, not from training
Keep the fine-tune for the staff's tone and style only
Repeating the run per change costs each time and leaves a wrong gap; test a fixed question set after every change

recall.model: Keep the fine-tune for the voice and tone it was meant to teach, and stop relying on it for fees. Put the fee list in a current, dated source and look up the right entry at question time, handing it to the model with the question and asking it to quote the fee with its date. Repeating the run after each change costs money every time and leaves customers with the wrong fee for the whole gap, weeks each time. Keep a fixed set of questions, including fee questions, and run it after every change, before and after, so you see the score move.

recall.prompt: On Bevis's 20 questions, with 6 on rules changed since March, what do the March fine-tune alone and lookup in the council's dated page score?
options: Fine-tune 14 of 20; with the page 19 of 20
Fine-tune 19 of 20; with the page 14 of 20
Fine-tune 6 of 20; with the page 20 of 20
recall.why: The fine-tune gets the 14 unchanged rules right and all 6 changed ones wrong: every answer it learned from was written before June. Lookup gets all 6 right and misses one, the cut-through, because the page calls it Cordwainer Row.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: we trained our model on our own experts' answers, so it knows our business better than any document could. When is fine-tuning the right tool, and when the wrong one?

keyIdeas.idea: Right for behaviour: tone, format, a narrow job a small model should do cheaply
Wrong for facts that change or must be cited: they stay as they were at training time
Prove it with a score on a fixed set of questions before and after, and combine with lookup

recall.model: Fine-tuning is the right tool for behaviour: tone, format, the way your experts explain things, or getting a small model to do one narrow job cheaply. It is the wrong tool for facts that change or must be cited, because the model keeps them as they were at training time, and only another run updates them; those belong in the prompt or a lookup, with their date. The two combine well. And don't take it on trust: score the model on a fixed set of questions before and after every change, including questions on facts that changed.

recall.prompt: Retraining Pennethorne's assistant costs about $400 and three weeks of checking each time, and the council changed 5 rules in two years. Retraining after each change, what does that come to over two years?
options: $2,000 and about 105 days of wrong answers
$400 and about 21 days of wrong answers
$1,200 and about 63 days of wrong answers
recall.why: 5 changes at $400 is $2,000, and each leaves three weeks, 21 days, of wrong answers while the new answers are checked: 5 times 21 is 105 days. $1,200 and 63 days is only the 3 changes since March.

recall.prompt: Amazon Bedrock's user guide says that in supervised fine-tuning the model parameters are adjusted. For which tasks does it say performance improves?
options: The tasks represented by the training dataset
Every task the model is ever asked
Only tasks about events after training
Tasks described in the system prompt
recall.why: The guide says the model parameters are adjusted in the process and the model's performance is improved for the tasks represented by the training dataset. A rule that changes after the data was gathered isn't in it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. The lookup on the council's page has held. The council changed the bridge's width limit in January, and the assistant had it by the next morning. But on Monday 1 February Ptolemy raised our lesson price from $38 to $42 an hour. Two weeks later the assistant is still telling learners $38, in our friendliest voice. Ptolemy says it's time to retrain.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why does it still say $38, and what should Pennethorne do?

keyIdeas.idea: The price is a changing fact it learned from the fine-tune's answers, and lookup only covers the council's page
Put the school's own dated price list where the assistant looks things up or in its instructions, not into training
Add price questions to the test and run it after every change the school makes too

coldCase.model: It says $38 because the price was never moved out of training: the March answers mention it, and the lookup only covers the council's page, so the old price is still the only one it has. Retraining would fix it three weeks late and cost $400 again. Instead, keep a short, dated price list of the school's own and let the assistant look it up the same way it looks up the rules, or put the price in its instructions, since it is one line. Then add questions on the price to the test and run it after every change, including the school's own changes, not only the council's.

sources.title: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus and others, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks, arXiv 2005.11401 (submitted 22 May 2020), read 15 October 2026: Large pre-trained language models have been shown to store factual knowledge in their parameters, and achieve state-of-the-art results when fine-tuned on downstream NLP tasks; However, their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is still limited, and hence on knowledge-intensive tasks, their performance lags behind task-specific architectures; providing provenance for their decisions and updating their world knowledge remain open research problems
